Then we have this amendment:
Annual interest accruing within the taxation period in respect of succession duties or inheritance taxes;
Section 5 is the section.
Oh, I beg your pardon. That makes a vast difference. That is why I could not follow the minister at all.

I should like to ask a question in connection with the interest charged on income tax, and this is the only section on which 1 can ask it. I should like to find out from the minister the various interest rates charged by the government on all income tax. I think they amount to usury. This government borrows money for its own purposes at two-thirds of one per cent. Why should it charge the people, under this and all the other sections, a high rate of interest on deferred payments, amounting to usury? In the second place, what about the time of payment? I suggest that after the winter, when people have not the money with which to pay their coal and other bills, is the wrong time to collect; a later month would do. I believe there should be more divisible payments such as the municipalities have. There should be easier terms of payment and less interest and other charges.

Two years ago, I think, the rate was reduced from six per cent to five per cent, and the penalty interest was reduced from four per cent to three per cent. I think that is as far as the government can reasonably be expected to go.
It amounts to usury.

I should like to follow up the question of the hon. member for York South. Assume the case of a dispute between an estate and the succession duties office covering a period of three years. At the end of that period interest is charged for two years and six months, or whatever time the law allows under the succession duties act of the province. The income tax has been paid in previous years; we come to the third year, when a deduction has to be made covering the entire period. We cannot deduct the full amount in any one year. We have paid the income tax for the two previous years. Is it possible to get a rebate covering the interest paid during those first two years, which cannot be deducted in the third year, though the income tax has been paid?

There is a limitation section which would make it difficult if the facts
were as stated by the hon. gentleman; but it is very easy to prevent the limitation section from applying, by the taxpayer simply reserving his rights. The taxpayer knows he has not paid his succession duties; he knows he is going to pay them some time or other, and in making his return he only needs to make some claim for a deduction in respect to succession duties. Then two or three years later, whenever he reaches a settlement, he can obtain a deduction in respect to that particular year. Because of that one year limitation he has to reserve his rights.

If he does not make
that reservation in his return he has lost his right to get any relief?

That is right. Everyone is
in the same position.

That does not make it
right. A wrong is all the greater if we are all done an injustice.

I do not admit that it is
a wrong. People must be a bit alert in making out their returns.

I would say they must
be very alert and must anticipate many things they can hardly be expected to foresee or know. Disputes with the succession duties office cover a long period of time, and their attitude is so arbitrary and in many cases so unreasonable that no executor can anticipate what is going to happen. He should be able to get an adjustment within six months, but he has to await the pleasure of that office. They keep him dallying around, and even though he has made a deposit they allow him no interest on it. In the end they make their valuation on an arbitrary basis; he has to pay a large amount of money and apparently can get no relief.
Let us assume that the succession duties office of Ontario, or of any other province, comes along after a period of ten, fifteen or twenty years, after an estate has been wound up, the succession duties paid and a receipt obtained for them. They say, "We are going to reopen and revalue this estate," as they have done. They increase the value, increase the duties, apply interest for ten, fifteen or twenty years and on top of that impose penalties. What is going to happen by way of getting a rebate of the interest that has been paid or has to be paid on this basis? Is the limitation to apply there, and will the department say, "I am sorry, but we cannot do anything for you?" How could a man possibly have anticipated, when making his in-
Income War Tax Act

come return in a case of that kind, that the succession duties branch was going to come along after ten years, reopen the estate, revalue it, charge interest on it and exact penalties? A person would have no reason to anticipate that action. We will say that it might amount to a million dollars.

But surely that is not our
responsibility. If a province acts arbitrarily the dominion government cannot be asked to make up the loss or the disadvantage.

That is not the point.
At the present time the dominion government comes in arbitrarily and says, "We are going to do the same as the province; to the devil with the taxpayer."

The dominion says, "We are hot going to make you any allowance at all, although you have to pay the interest." And then this particular province takes the tax based upon income tax returns made during these years-the same province.

The hon. member apparently thinks that the interest between 1920 and 1930 would be a proper deduction from the income of the year 1938-39. But that does not appeal to me as being a proper deduction. It is not a deduction from the income of 1938 or 1939; but it is the interest paid during that year that is a proper deduction.
Will assessments be reopened? Will there be a deduction, an allowance or a rebate over the period of five or ten years back? Or is a person entirely shut off by the limitation?
He is shut off.
I thought so, and I think it is very unfair.

If we went back and opened up income tax returns for the last twenty years because of everything that someone might discover, we would be opening them up all the time. That is the reason for the limitation.
But you are opening them for ten years because the government takes the notion to do it. You go back ten years and open up cases where assessment has been made?
Yes.
You do it, but the taxpayer cannot do it.
The information is in the hands of the taxpayer, not in the hands of the government.

In this case the information is not in the hands of the taxpayer at all. He has given all the information and has acted in good faith in the whole matter. Then it is reopened, after it is supposed to be closed.
His quarrel is with the province that reopens it, not with us.
His quarrel is with this government, that is taking income tax from him, when he is compelled out of this income to pay interest.
I do not know whether it is out of income or not.
Where else would it come from?
It is out of his money.
It is out of his income.
Or capital, or both.
It is out of his income, and if he could show for that year that he paid the interest for that particular year he would get a deduction.
Yes.
Then why should it not be possible for him to go back over the years and get a refund?
That is a different question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 6 carry?

I do not suppose it is
worth while to bring this matter to a vote, but I certainly wish to go on record as strongly opposed to this provision, and I think it ought to be given a great deal of consideration before it is passed. It is unfair to people who have no control over the situation. I have in mind at the moment an estate where the mother of the deceased, who was entirely dependent upon the deceased for support, will receive a comparatively modest annual income. There will come a time when three or four years' interest will have to be paid to the succession duties branch in Ontario, on some amount of money, when that amount of money is ascertained. What is paid will be deducted from the income of that widowed mother. And the same thing will apply to the child, who is now twelve years of age and is being maintained in school through a trust fund. The widowed mother and the child of the

Income War Tax Act
deceased are to be asked to pay income tax on income they never received, never could receive and never will receive. It is entirely contrary to the principle of this type of legislation.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Limitation of salary deduction.

Has consideration been
given to the question whether or not nonresident investment corporations would be excluded from the operations of the section by the words "unless such non-resident pays tax thereon under this act"?
It applies to all of them.
Does it apply to nonresident-owned investment corporations?
Yes.

Some few years ago, with a view to bringing foreign capital to this country, we enacted provisions in our Income War Tax Act relative to non-resident-owned investment corporations. As a result a good deal of foreign capital came to this country, based on the provisions of the act as it then stood. The dominion obtains a tax on the income of a non-resident-owned investment corporation, and I imagine the total amount obtained annually is substantial. By reason of a non-resident-owned investment corporation having power to pay out its funds to non-residents in the form of directors' salaries, and so on, rather than in the form of dividends, a great deal of foreign capital was induced to come to this country. It would seem to me that this enactment would simply reverse the position we took in 1935 or 1936. As the government gets the tax anyway, no matter in what form a non-resident-owned investment corporation pays out its income, I can see no reason for making this amendment applicable to non-resident-owned investment corporations.
Oh, no.
The people who bring their money here to invest in non-resident-owned investment corporations bring their money here to keep. This is not a high-salaried field.

Let us be honest and frank about it. As I have said, our reason for enacting provisions in the Income War Tax Act with respect to non-resident-owned investment corporations was to induce a large amount of capital to come here from the United States. The action was taken at a time when President Roosevelt in connection with his new deal operations was enacting legislation in the United States and pyramiding taxes to the point where people who had money wanted to take care of it. With that in mind, with the desire to get money in Canada, we enacted provisions with respect to non-resident-owned investment corporations. When we did that we decided the rate of tax we wanted to get on the money, and we fixed that rate under our act. The government of this country gets the same amount of tax, irrespective of whether a non-resident-owned investment corporation pays out its money in salaries, dividends or directors' fees. It does not matter how the money is paid out.
I do not understand that. We tax the income at half the corporate rate. If the company pays $100,000 to its president in New York, it has an effect on the income.

The income of a nonresident-owned investment corporation is determined not by what it pays out but by what it takes in. The rates for a non-resident-owned investment corporation are half the corporate rates for a domestic corporation.
But on the net income.
Is it on the net?
Certainly.
All I have to say is-
I thought it was.

As a matter of practical demonstration, I have in mind a non-resident-owned investment corporation whose solicitor wanted deliberately to pay out money in the form of salaries and not in the form of dividends. This was not done with a view to taking any money away from the government of Canada; they simply wanted to do it in that way in order to get money into the hands of non-residents in another country for their tax benefit in that country. That nonresident-owned investment corporation has never deducted the salaries which it has paid before paying the tax here.

I shall have to go into that; I am afraid it is a surprise to me. I thought we taxed, and the commissioner tells me that we taxed, the net income of these companies. If a salary of $100,000 is paid, that would cut down the income to that extent and we would get that much less tax.
Income War Tax Act

I quite agree that under our present act that $100,000 could be paid out to a non-resident in salary and deducted as an expense of operation before the tax was received by the government, but I do not think that that is what happens in practice. In fact the non-resident-owned investment corporation pays the tax before paying out any money in the form of salaries.
My information is to the contrary, and I am surprised to hear that.
Except what is paid to a book-keeper or someone of that kind.

Section agreed to.
On section 9-Limit of deduction.

Would the minister give a specific instance or an illustration as to just what this amendment will apply? It strikes me that this is another amendment like 32b which we had last year. We were told in the House of Commons that that meant one thing; then the minister stated in the newspapers that it meant another thing, and later the commissioner came out with a statement that it meant something else. I do not think many of us are certain yet as to what 32b does mean.

The trouble with 32b was in the understanding of members of the house; there was no difference between the commissioner and the minister as to what it meant. I was entirely unable to see why there should be any misunderstanding as to what 32b meant.
If I had time to go upstairs and get the file I could read both statements and leave it to the committee to consider whether there was any misunderstanding.
They agreed absolutely.
Could the minister give an illustration of what set of circumstances this is designed to meet?

I have some examples here for the purpose of answering this question, but perhaps I had better give it in my own words. A company may have a non-taxable income of $1,000,000, which non-taxable income would be income derived from dividends paid by Canadian corporations which had themselves paid income tax. These dividends would not be taxable again as income in the hands of the receiving corporation. The company has a taxable income of $1,000,000, which taxable income might be made up of interest on bonds or profits from industrial, commercial or financial undertakings. From those two
f Mr. Ilgley.]
sources of income, the company has a gross income of $2,000,000. Let us assume the expenses of operation are $750,000.
Say $1,000,000 and make it simple.

The company has expenses of operation totalling $1,000,000. With a gross income of $2,000,000, this would leave a net income of $1,000,000. In the past this company would come to the commissioner of income tax and say, "The $1,000,000 we have in income is non-taxable income and therefore we owe you nothing." This amendment makes that practice impossible. The amendment is based upon the theory that part of the $1,000,000 expense would probably be incurred in earning the non-taxable income as well as the taxable, and therefore there should be an allotment of expenses to the non-taxable and taxable incomes.
On what basis?
On the basis set by the minister.
Is the minister to have discretionary power to set the basis, or is it to be as the non-taxable is to the taxable?

It is not ratable. The resolution had it ratable, but I moved to have that struck out. It would not be fair in many cases. This is one of those sections which are most undesirable from my point of view, but I do not know in what other way it can be done. Undoubtedly the principle is right and I think it will have to be left to someone, probably the minister, to allot the expenses between the two kinds of income.

I am not so sure that the principle is right. It may be right in some cases, but I do not think it would be right in others. Let me give an illustration. I know a company which has thirty-seven subsidiaries, every one of which is an operating company, some making money and others losing money. Those that make money pay a tax. The parent company is also a large operating company, doing a larger business than the consolidated business of the thirty-seven subsidiaries. The parent company receives dividends from some of the subsidiaries which have already paid the tax, and this income is non-taxable. In the case of the parent company I admit that an infinitesimal part of some book-keeper's time may be taken up in connection with the dividends from the subsidiary companies, but I venture to suggest that not more than one per cent of the overhead expenses of the parent com-

Income War Tax Act
pany could be referable to the operations of the subsidiaries. Is it worth while bringing this in in connection with such a company? Has the minister in mind certain companies where the overhead expenses of the parent company for the benefit of subsidiary companies is very substantial as compared with the overhead for its own operations?

There are cases. In the case mentioned by my hon. friend, if one per cent was found to be the proportion of the cost of earning and collecting the taxable income, one per cent is all that would be allotted. There would be no injustice. It is essential that these discretionary powers should be given. Hon. members of the house have paid tribute to the commissioner, and I think it is widely conceded that he exercises his powers quite fairly.

We all agree with that.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

The last three lines of section 8 are:
Where general expenses are incurred to earn both taxable and non-taxable income the minister shall have power to apportion the said expenses.
The point I wish to make is that no minister of the crown should have these powers and prerogatives under a bill such as this, a revenue bill. Parliament is thereby delegating to the minister certain powers under which the regulations he makes will have the force of law. This clause delegating power to the minister is similar to one of the sections which was condemned down at Washington, where after an elaborate senate inquiry it was found that, by such a provision in their bill, many millionaires had escaped income taxation altogether. It is not necessary to give their names, but millionaires and their companies worth hundreds of millions of dollars were able by this route to evade payment of income tax. I make no reflection upon the minister, or upon his able, painstaking and capable deputy, Mr. Elliott. But it seems to me that very few concessions are given to the small man; and in my opinion a national revenue committee of the house should be set up to go into this whole question of national revenue and of the powers of the minister and the delegation to the minister of the right to make rules and regulations along these lines. The committee might inquire into all kinds of sources of additional revenue, irregularities, exemptions, tax evasions, tax dodging, and all that. Further,
there should be incorporated into the statute amendments to make the committee's findings effective. I believe that if a national inquiry were to be held into this question in Canada, as was done at Washington, it would be a national calamity to read about.
No minister of the crown should be given the powers contained in the latter part of this section. I regret that this bill was brought down in the dying days of the session, when there is no time for a proper and adequate discussion of national revenue in all its forms and methods. Revenue and income are the most important things we have, and there should be some more modern way of debating so important a subject than the stereotyped process of bringing in at the end of a long session a bill of many sections along these lines. I repeat that I hope a proper independent inquiry for all Canada will be held to find out who is paying and who is not, and into all methods and practices. I should like to have from the minister some reply to indicate what is being done.

I dealt just before one o'clock with that point of the minister's discretion. I said that I was sorry to see in this bill sections which add to the minister's discretion, but there is no way I can think of by which they can be avoided. When we first drafted this resolution we provided for a ratable, a proportionate, distribution of expenses between non-taxable and taxable income, but on reexamination it was found that that would be unfair, that it was entirely too inflexible. The experience of the department has been that the very persons who complain about the extent of the minister's discretion, when they are confronted by an inflexible rule, hold up their hands in horror and say, "That leads to unfair results; something must be left to discretion, to the judgment of the official,"-the minister, in this case.

In the first place, I want to correct something I said this morning with respect to section 7. I was in error, apparently, in what I had to say with regard to nonresident-owned investment corporations. We had presented to us this morning a bill, nearly every clause of which had not 'been suggested either by the budget speech or by the resolutions in ways and means committee, and several provisions of which amount to straight increases in taxation under the Income War Tax Act; therefore we are trying to struggle through the bill without having had an opportunity to give it previous study.
With respect to section 8, the one specifically before the committee at the moment, I am
Income War Tax Act

soijry that I have to disagree with the hon. member for Broadview and to agree in large measure with the Minister of National Revenue. From my short experience in that office I realize that the Income War Tax Act simply cannot be administered without a wide measure of discretion in respect of many matters. But although I am not objecting in principle t.o the conferring of a discretionary power, the minister cannot in the exercise of that discretion run contrary to some definite principle which may be stated in the act. This brings me to a specific discussion of the section now under consideration.
During the adjournment I had an opportunity to sit down and do a little thinking, and I worked out what I think will be an example of how this will operate. If I am not correct I shall be glad to have the minister correct me.
I am going to take the example of a company which has five subsidiaries. I will call the parent company, company A and the subsidiaries, V, W, X, Y and Z. Each of these subsidiaries is carrying on a similar line of business. Each one annually files a return; and let me assume they have a profit and are paying income tax. What is left of their income after payment of tax goes to the parent company A. Under the present law that income, having been taxed once in the hands of the other company, and being taxed again when it is distributed by the parent company to the shareholders, is exempt from taxation as income in the hands of the parent company. Now, the parent company carries on a business similar to that of the five subsidiaries, and for the purpose of the business of the five subsidiaries it is necessary to have in the head office of the parent company, and associated with it, four officials. The specific duties of these four officials relate in a small measure to the parent company and in a large measure to the five subsidiaries. No deduction is made for their salaries when the income tax return is made by the five subsidiary companies. Let me assume their aggregate salaries amount to $20,000 a year. What result will we get after this legislation is passed?
In the first place let me assume that the income passing from the five subsidiaries to the parent company, and which is non-taxable income in the hands of the parent company, is $100,000. Let me assume that the parent company at the present time from its own operations has an income of $100,000, and that the expense, including the salary of the four officials most of whose time is spent looking after the general affairs of the subsidiaries, is $80,000. At the present time the parent company is paying income tax on a taxable

income of $20,000; the subsidiaries are paying income tax on a taxable income which after payment of the tax is $100,000. How is the minister going to exercise his discretion once this section goes through? It is my submission that he must exercise it in one of two ways. If the minister says, because the gross income of the parent is $100,000 and the net income of the subsidiaries is $100,000, therefore the expenses of the operation of the parent company should be divided fifty per cent to each, the result will be that the parent company will have to pay on a taxable income of $60,000 instead of $20,000.
I cannot follow the arithmetic. That first way is out-or it may be out.

Well, we shall see. Be
careful that I do not confront you with a past decision. Let me assume that the minister takes the only other course which, so far as I can see, is open to him. He says: No, the fair way to exercise this discretion is as follows. Because the aggregate salaries of these four officials is $20,000, and because their time is devoted almost entirely to the subsidiaries, their salaries should be set aside as against the non-taxable income. By reason of that you automatically reduce the expenses of the parent company from $80,000 for the year to $60,000, and thereby you automatically double the taxable income of the parent company, from $20,000 a year to $40,000 a year. Does the minister follow my figures? If I am correct in that, what are you doing in the result?
I admit that there are in this country those who think that double taxation in respect of the same money is justifiable. Personally I do not; I never have, and I have no hesitation in saying so, no matter who likes it or who does not.
It is triple in this case.

I think that the principle of taxing money in the hands of the corporation and then taxing it over again in the hands of the shareholders is wrong. Income should be taxed once, and once only. The resplt of this proposed legislation is that, no matter how fair the minister tries to be, no matter in what way he exercises his discretion, part of that income is taxed three times. True, the third taxation is by the indirect method of taking some of the expenses of the parent company and saying, "This should be set aside against the non-taxable income."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They never were expenses of the parent company.

When I took the illustration of five subsidiaries I took a small com-

pany; but the corporation I have in mind has, I venture to suggest, more than fifty subsidiaries. Their principle of operation has always been this. They charge no expenses to the subsidiary-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But they should.

Wait a minute. They
cannot, for this reason. To. do that you would have to try to segregate that portion of the time of the four executives of the parent company which is devoted to the interests of the subsidiaries and then charge against the subsidiaries a proportion of their salary and have these men receive their salaries in fifty pieces, fifty cheques, from fifty subsidiaries. The thing is simply not reasonable or feasible, but for the purposes of operation of their subsidiaries it is essential to have these four officials in the head office. No matter how the minister exercises his discretion, if this subsection is passed the net result will be to triple taxation on a part of the earnings of the combined subsidiary and parent companies. I do not care how the discretion is exercised, that will be the result. The parent company has an income of, say, $100,000 from its subsidiaries, which is therefore non-taxable, and the parent company earns from its own operations, in exactly the same business as the subsidiaries, another $100,000 gross income. The parent company's expenses of operations are $80,000 a year, but included in this $80,000 are the salaries of four officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the point.

But most of their time
is devoted necessarily to the operation of the subsidiaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Why should they not
be charged to the subsidiaries?

For the simple reason
that it is a cumbersome method of doing it. Let me answer the minister's question with another:	Why should this government pass
a law which would make it necessary for business concerns to charge to subsidiaries a proportion of salaries which are payable in the head office for people who work in the head office, and have the subsidiaries pay these people their salaries in fifty pieces if there are fifty subsidiary companies?

So that the companies will
not be able to avoid paying taxes on taxable income.
But they are not avoiding paying taxes on taxable income. How are they doing so?

By charging to taxable
income expenses incurred in earning nontaxable income.
The reason it is nontaxable income in the hands of the parent company is that it was taxable income in the hands of the subsidiaries. You have already had your tax on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If there is expense in
connection with it, that should have been deducted before the original tax was determined.

Granted; and if that were done you would get the same result as you are getting now. In other words, this government is now receiving income tax from the subsidiaries without deducting the expenses of four officials in the head office, and to that extent the tax it is getting from the parent company is reduced; but it is still getting a tax. Why pass legislation the result of which is to require that a large corporation, four of whose executive officials are now being paid salaries by the parent company, shall split up their salaries into small pieces and have each subsidiary contribute to those salaries?
There is no difficulty about that.

It may not be difficult to
the minister, but it is difficult to the company; and it is absurd to ask a large enterprise to issue fifty separate weekly or monthly cheques as the case may be, from fifty separate and distinct companies.
They could issue one cheque and charge the right proportion to each subsidiary.

That would be simple if
they were making a consolidated return, but they are not making a consolidated return; they are making individual returns. If these companies were making a consolidated return for income tax purposes, I agree that it would be very simple; but they are not. If they made a consolidated return they would have to pay an extra two per cent-17 per cent instead of 15 per cent-and to avoid that they make individual returns. Is it fair? Is there any reason why the government should put business in this country to that additional trouble and expense if the minister is going to exercise his discretion along the line he indicates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member has stated one hypothetical cane: nav I put

another. I have not worked it out as he has put it. He has made out a case for inconvenience. as I see it. I must make out a case for necessity, the necessity for this change. Instead of the proportions which he took, assume a parent with a laTge non-taxable subsidiary income, a parent who, having watched very carefully the mechanics of the operation of this law, has found that if it charges to itself the expenses of officers and overhead, which really are concerned with the subsidiaries, it thereby escapes a charge against income, 'because that income is nontaxable, having been taxed once. My hon. friend assumed an ordinary industrial case. If you take the minimum of industry and the maximum of investment, you can readily visualize why it is that the income tax administration requires some means of checking what really amounts to the transferring of subsidiary expenses to the parent.

Let me take the minister's illustration and follow it up. The minister takes the case of minimum of industry and maximum of investment. Will he not agree with me that in the head office of that parent company the only work required to look after the investment income would be the time of a book-keeper in entering that income into the ledgers and books of the parent company? If its industrial operations are part of its enterprise I think the minister will agree that the overhead would be tremendous as compared to the mere overhead of collecting investment income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely, that is the whole point.

If that is the whole point, as the overhead for the industrial phase, which is the minimum, is the large proportion of the overhead, is it not right and proper that the expense of that overhead should be charged against the income of the parent company, which is taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Wherever the expense is incurred, there it should be taxed.
If that is so, what do you accomplish by this section, if the situation is as the Minister of Finance outlined it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are going to see, with respect to a parent which is small in operation industrially speaking but large in ownership of investment income, particularly in the form of dividends-because the same thing does not apply if it is interest income; my hon. friend knows that-

Right.
[Mr. Dunning.;

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -that it shall not be possible, shall I say, to inflate the volume of expenses which may be charged against taxable income. That is a means of preventing the inflation of that book-keeper into a much larger expense than merely a book-keeper.
But you already have power to do that under the act. The income in the hands of the parent is non-taxable because the subsidiary has already paid taxes in respect to that income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

If you now propose to take a part of an expense actually incurred in the head office and set that over against nontaxable income so that it cannot be deducted as an expense against taxable income, are you not in truth and in fact collecting more tax from that corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see that.

Well, I am sorry to say I cannot see otherwise. You are in effect collecting triple tax, because by setting some expenses over against non-taxable income you are increasing the taxable income of the parent company and thereby in effect, in my opinion, taxing the same money three times.

Section agreed to.
On section 9-Limit of deduction.

This in my opinion is
another instance of increasing taxation by the method of introducing a bill of this kind. This section is so involved that I have great difficulty in following it; will the minister explain what its effect will be?

Let us assume that we are dealing with a taxpayer who is a resident of this country and who has an income of 8100,000, of which $25,000 is derived from a foreign source-say the United States, although it would apply to any foreign country. Canada imposes an individual income tax on the income of $100,000. But the United States has imposed a tax on $25,000 of that income in the country of origin. By one of the sections of the Income War Tax Act, I think section 8, a taxpayer when he comes to pay his income tax to us is entitled to a credit of the tax that he has paid in the United States up to the amount of our rate. The question arises, what is our rate? Our rate varies, depending upon the size of the income. And we have said that we take the average rate here-

Excuse me; that is what I do not understand. I understand the min-

Income War Tax Act
ister when he tells me what the law now is. Would he start again from there on?

We take the average rate
as opposed to the rate in the top of the bracket or at the lower end of the scale. For instance, it may be that the rate paid on the $25,000 in the foreign country is more than the rate-
More than the tax which would have been payable in Canada?

More than the tax that
would be payable at the average rate in Canada.
I cannot find "average rate" anywhere in here.

Let us read the section:
Subsection 2 of section 8 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
(2) Such deduction shall not exceed the same proportion of the tax otherwise payable under this act as that which the taxpayer's net income from sources within such country (that is the foreign country) bears to his entire net income from all sources-
I do not think the rest touches the subject.
-without taking into account the exemptions
Now what does that mean, what the minister has just read?

Perhaps I had better let that go until I get a little further explanation. The principle of the section is that the taxpayer claims that he has a right to take the rate applicable to the last $25,000 of his income, and we say he cannot take that. But I shall have to take a specific case and give it a little later. It is very complicated. Shall wye let the clause stand?

Let us see whether the minister and I agree on what the present law means. As the law is now, if I have an income from a foreign country, the tax upon which income in Canada is $90, but there has already been $100 deducted from me in the foreign country, I then pay no tax on that income in Canada. Are we correct in that? In other words, at the present time, having computed the Canadian income tax payable on my whole income I am entitled to deduct from that tax the tax I paid upon any portion of that income in a foreign country, with a limit. The limit is that I cannot deduct more than the tax I would have to pay in Canada if I had not paid in the foreign country.
Yes, but the dispute arises just there; what is the tax on that $25,000 in this country in the case I put?
I have been dealing with tax, not income.

I do not want any misunderstanding. The taxpayer is likely to say that the tax on that $25,000 is very high in Canada, because you must take the tax at the top of the scale. We say, No, you cannot do that, you cannot take the tax at the top. The tax on the last $25,000 may be thirty or forty per cent. He will therefore say the tax in Canada was more than $100 and therefore he must have the whole $100 allowed as a credit against the tax in Canada. To that we say: No, you do not take what you would pay on $25,000 at the top bracket; we take in that case one-quarter of the total tax you pay, and we say the Canadian tax is twenty-five one hundredths.
The minister is now dealing with the new proposal?
Yes.
I was trying to get an agreement on what the law now is.

I think the hon. gentleman has correctly stated the law as it is, but I am showing the disputes that may arise and have arisen as to the extent of the credit that the dominion government is obliged to give that particular taxpayer under the law as it now stands without this change. The taxpayer will submit that his Canadian tax on the $25,000 is high, perhaps thirty or forty per cent, because he assumes that the $25,000 is his top $25,000, the last that he earned, the amount that takes him into the high bracket. We are just as much entitled to say it is the first $25,000, but that would not be fair either. If that were the case his Canadian tax might be only $10, and we might give him credit for only $10, which might not be fair. The only fair thing is to put the average tax at the proportion of the total tax that the foreign earned income bears to the total income.

But is it necessary that we should go to that extent? Our interests in Canada are what the Canadian taxpayer has received from his foreign investments; and irrespective of the laws applicable with respect to income tax in that foreign country, would it not be fairer to say that the net result of any investment we have in that foreign country will be merged with my domestic income, and then, after all the deductions that have been allowed in that foreign country, I will
Income War Tax Act

be taxed on the basis of the net income resulting from my investment? I may be all wrong in my interpretation of the wording of this section, but I am afraid it is going to work havoc with the Canadian taxpayer. Irrespective of the foreign law, it seems to me what the Canadian government should be interested in is the net income the Canadian taxpayer received in Canada. Therefore, if the income from foreign investments has been allowed certain deductions in foreign countries, we should not be interested or concerned in correcting those deductions. We should simply take the net result to the taxpayer in Canada, merge that with his domestic income, and then apply the general schedule.

But, Mr. Chairman, if that plan were followed in the case outlined by the minister the Canadian taxpayer would be penalized to a greater extent than under the suggestion made by the minister. Obviously the 825,000 income from a foreign country would be taxed in the lower brackets of that country, but when added to his 875,000 earned in Canada he would be open to taxation in this country on the basis of 8100,000. But if I understood the minister correctly this means that instead of the department allowing him a deduction only on the lowest bracket, namely the rate on 825,000, or granting him the privilege of putting it in the highest bracket, the rate on 8100,000, they propose to strike a compromise between the two and allow a deduction equal to the rate on say $50,000. It is quite conceivable that if the course suggested by my hon. friend were to be followed the taxpayer would receive a lower credit than he would obtain by striking an average.
Is that correct?
That is what I gathered from the remarks of the minister.
I did not understand it in that way.

If I followed my hon. friend correctly, he has in mind that we may not allow' as much as is paid in the foreign country. I shall have to go over this again; I find difficulty in following hon. gentlemen because they start from new and unthought of points of view.
Stick to your total income of 8100,000, with $25,000 coming from a foreign country.

I shall go through this explanation again. If I understood him aright the hon. member for York South was correct in the proposition he laid down, that if in

respect of the foreign earned income the taxpayer must pay a tax of $100, we give him a credit of 8100 here, but that credit shall not be greater than the amount of the Canadian tax on an income of 825,000. But then the question arises, at what rate? The Canadian tax varies. If he had only $25,000 his tax rate here might be very low, and therefore he would not get a credit of 8100.
If I may interrupt the minister at this point, is it not a question of deduction rather than a question of rate, under section 9?
This is a deduction of tax, not a deduction from income.
That is why I cannot understand what the rate has to do with it.

It is a method of getting at the same result; it is a way of coming to the conclusion expressed in the section. To go over the case again, the income from all sources is $100,000, with $25,000 earned in the United States.
That is, a gross income of $25,000 earned in the United States?
Yes.
Before the United States has made any deduction for tax?

Yes. Let us say there is a tax in the United States of $100. That figure may be totally unrelated to an income of $25,000; I do not know, but we will say the tax is $100. Our law says that when he comes to pay his income tax here he is to have that $100 deducted from the tax he pays us. It is not a deduction from income; it is a deduction from the tax, but the deduction shall not be more than the tax Canada would have imposed on that S25,000. The question then arises, how much tax would Canada have imposed? Well, it depends upon whether you consider that to be his first $25,000 or his last $25,000, whether it is at the bottom or the top of the scale. The taxpayer will come along and say it is at the top of the scale. The rate at the top is high; the tax here would have been $150, we will say, and therefore the taxpayer says he is entitled to credit for the entire $100. We may say, "That is not so. You are entitled to credit for only $10." What we say here, however, is that we will take what I described previously as an average rate. That is not strictly technically correct, but that is what it comes to. We say we will take the proportion of that which the income earned in the foreign country bears to the total income from all sources. We will

Income War Tax Act
take that proportion of the tax and say that is the tax Canada would have levied on the $25,000.
But will not the result be that the deductions allowed in foreign countries may be reduced with respect to the Canadian income tax, more than otherwise would be the case?
Correct.
Why should not the deductions that are allowed in foreign countries be allowed for income tax purposes in this country?

Section 8 makes it clear that that is not the law. The rates may be high in foreign countries. We do not allow foreign countries, by putting up their rates, to take all our income tax away from us. The deduction can be only up to the tax that Canada would impose; otherwise we should be at the mercy of foreign governments.
But would not the better way be, with respect to a Canadian taxpayer, to take the net results of his foreign income?
Of his Canadian income?

A Canadian taxpayer receiving income from foreign investments should declare to the Canadian collector the net results of his foreign investments, as part of his income. Would that not be a much fairer basis than by dickering with the deductions allowed in foreign countries?
I do not think so.

My opinion is that the Canadian government should be concerned only in this way: "Here is a Canadian taxpayer; what is his net income?" And if all that income, instead of being from foreign investment, were from domestic investment, that income shall be taxed under the schedules provided under the Canadian law respecting income tax? That is my view of it. I would say, irrespective of what other countries prescribe in respect of deductions: "What is the net result to you as a taxpayer from your foreign investments?" Then if the yield from the foreign investment or the net result is so many thousand dollars, those thousands of dollars involved are merged into the Canadian income.
That is double taxation.
Would that be the result?
Yes, both countries would be taxing, and it would not be fair.
I do not see it.
Leaving aside all legal cobwebs, may I ask the minister if the purpose of the law is not that of encouraging investment in Canada?
No, it is to take more money out of the income tax payer.
That feature is now in the act, of course, and especially in relation to the non-resident-owned investment corporation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report the bill?

I want to make one or two general comments with respect to this bill. I made a statement in this house in discussing the budget as to the quantum of taxation being collected by this government. I took occasion to point out that they have been the greatest tax collectors in the history of Canada. Some hon. member on the other side, following me, took occasion to point out that there were no tax increases in the budget of this year. I should like to pause here to make it clear that although no tax increases were indicated in the budget of this year, the

Income War Tax Act
net result of this bill is further to increase the taxation upon the people of this country, by sections 6, 8 and 9 of the bill if not by others. Amendments of the kind contained in this bill, constituting changes in the income tax, excise or other tax statutes, should be clearly set out in the budget proposals of the Minister of Finance. They should not, as in this case, come as a whole series of amendments affecting taxation imposed upon the people, tied on to one single thing mentioned by the Minister of Finance in his budget and to one single resolution that went before the ways and means committee, having to do with the proposed exemption from taxation in respect of construction costs. It is important that it be recorded in Hansard that though we were led to believe that the net result of the budget proposals would be a reduction in taxation to stimulate construction through the amendments to the Income War Tax Act contained in this bill, the government is making a valiant effort to take out of other income tax payers the contemplated reduction in taxation affecting those who embark upon new construction.

The sections the hon. gentleman referred to were Nos. 6, 8 and 9. Section 9 makes no increase in taxation; it is a clarifying section. speechtext:
I have no objection to
making an explanation, although I believe that most of the necessary explanation was given when the resolution upon which the bill is based was accepted by the house. I would point out again, however, that under the bill it is intended to provide for the
constitution of a board to help the export of salt fish from Canada. It is well known to those who live in the provinces adjoining the Atlantic coast that most of the fishermen are interested in processing their fish by salting it for market and export purposes. Compared with the total production, only a small quantity is consumed in Canada. Most of it is exported to foreign countries.
In the last few years the countries to which we used to export fish have been difficult to deal with. For instance, at one time Italy offered a valuable market for our fish from the north shore of New Brunswick and the Gaspe coast, but to-day Italy is completely lost as a market for fish. All this has taken place as a result of conditions over which we have had no control and which at the present time would be difficult to correct. Spain at one time absorbed considerable quantities of salt fish, but to-day, for reasons over which we have no control, the markets in Spain have been absolutely closed to our fish.
In past years South America and the West Indies offered a market for the great part of our salt fish, but, for reasons better known to some other hon. members, our facilities for marketing in South American countries are not as good as they were. In many of those countries our products have been removed from the market, and the opportunity to sell our fish has been greatly reduced.
We have been able to market a considerable quantity of salt fish in the West Indies, but, as is well known, the purchasing power of the people of the West Indies is low, and our fishermen do not obtain a return sufficient to cover even the cost of production, which in recent years has been dropped to a very low point.
Our fishermen have been unable to export the product of their labours and have not succeeded in obtaining returns sufficient to support themselves and their families. As a result they are asking the government for help.
Another factor worthy of consideration is that of the competition from foreign countries which have established organized methods of marketing, through governmental or semigovernmental agencies, and have also bonused the processing and export of their dried fish. With all these factors to contend with, the house can readily see the difficulties our fishermen have to meet.
Some may contend that the fishermen should change their methods and revert to the production of fresh fish. However, fish

Salt Fish Board

is perishable product which cannot be kept very long. Along the north shore of the St. Lawrence, on the Gaspe coast, on the north shore of New Brunswick, in Prince Edward Island, on the east and west coasts of Nova Scotia, and around Cape Breton, the people live in small villages where there are no facilities for keeping fish fresh. At one time these people were able to live upon the returns of their fishing operations, but to-day they cannot sell their fish. Those who are fortunate enough to find an agency through which to dispose of their catch find that the return is not sufficient to support themselves andi their families. For years those connected with the fishing industry or those interested in the welfare of these people have tried to find means of coping with this situation. Suggestions have been made which have been carefully looked into and studied.
In 1938 the fisheries branch of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, eastern division, held a convention at Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, and passed a resolution on September 12, 1938, containing the following paragraph: In the sections of coast not favoured with rapid transportation facilities affording access to fresh fish markets, salting, drying and pickling is the only means of taking care of surplus catches. Without a reasonably profitable outlet for fish in salted and dried state, there can be no general prosperity, even in a modest way, in the fisheries of the Atlantic coast. Much of the distress in many fishing districts in eastern Canada can be ascribed directly to the decrease in salt fish production and the low prices due to conditions in the foreign markets for such fish.
The fisheries committee of the Halifax board of trade has always taken a keen interest in the welfare of the fishermen and in the industry generally.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: I do not think so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
This committee has made recommendations during the course of the year, one of which was worded as follows:
It being obvious that a large number of our Atlantic coast fishermen are not in a position to market their production in a fresh state for domestic consumption, we are of the opinion that help to the fishermen must mostly be found through an effort to rehabilitate the export dried fish trade.
We have received representations from associations of fishermen in many parts of the eastern provinces. I have one dated April 19, 1939, from the fishermen's association at Caraquet, New Brunswick. This is a district where in the past large quantities of the best quality fish were produced and exported. This letter is in French, but my translation is:
We have still more than 600 quintals of dried codfish on hand, and we respectfully ask you to be kind enough to help us to market them. 
The northern part of New Brunswick used to produce large quantities of dried fish and the people were relatively prosperous when they could market their fish. The fishermen of Shippigan, New Brunswick, passed a resolution on February 8, 1939, containing the following:
Whereas many fishermen have not yet been able to sell their fish and have still large quantities on hand, we ask you to be kind enough to dispose of same.
The fishermen around Lower Caraquet, New Brunswick, used to be prosperous and produced large quantities of dried fish. The following letter was written on their behalf on February 21, 1939:
I am sorry to state that the conditions of our poor fishermen have not been improved since last year, although, on the whole, the catch has been satisfactory; however, prices were very low and a fairly large number of our fishermen have yet notable quantities of their fish on hand, without any prospects for sale in sight.
I have endeavoured to show by these quotations what is in the minds of these fishermen. I should like to quote now from a letter written by an individual fisherman at Bathurst, New Brunswick. This is dated April 6, 1939, and reads in part:
We are cod fishermen and our codfish taken last fall is still in our hands, unsold.
He concludes by asking the department to sell his fish. In view of the many requests received, the department felt that the time had come to organize some body to help these people. Therefore it was decided to recommend to the house the constitution of a salt fish 'board which would be made up of men expert in the business. Their duty will be to investigate and report upon the marketing of salt fish in export trade and to explore the possibilities of opening up new markets. They will advise and recommend to the minister a plan or plans for the exporting of salt fish. They will study and recommend various methods of curing, packing and marketing fish to meet the requirements of consumers in foreign countries, and they will generally direct the processing and marketing of salt fish. The board will also give assistance to these people in the form and manner that may be deemed expedient, but not exceeding twenty-five per cent of the market value of the fish at the time of export. To meet such cases as I have already stated to the house, the board may also act as agent for individual fishermen and producers to export their fish for them and pay over to them the returns.
I have already said that in my humble opinion this board is necessitated by the needs of the fishermen. On account of the location

Salt Fish Board
of these people, the conditions under which they have been 'brought up, and the conditions under which they are now living and trying to operate, and because of the competition they have to meet in foreign markets from countries that have already in existence boards such as we are trying to organize,
I feel it is the simple duty of this parliament to approve the suggestions which are. 'being made by the department and to pass this legislation.
It might be said that this board should take in all the fish trade-fresh as well as salt fish. Well, 'it might 'be an advantage to the individual fisherman if the government would undertake to sell all the fish which is being taken out of the ocean. But we feel that the fresh fish branch of the industry is not meeting so much competition as the salt fish branch. In fact, fresh fish caught in. Canada is sold, first in the local market, then in the United States or Great Britain; this applies mostly to all varieties of fresh fish including canned salmon, halibut, and frozen salmon from the Atlantic coast. In those markets our exporters and dealers in fresh fish do not meet the same amount of competition as dealers in salt fish have to face in foreign countries.
We have been helping indirectly in many ways the fresh fish industry. We have tried to increase consumption in our local markets; we have tried, by negotiating agreements and canvassing markets with the object of obtaining preference for the product of our own industry, to increase the volume of export to foreign countries. To market all the fish through a government agency would be difficult if not impossible of accomplishment and would simply add to our predicament by inducing people to catch more fresh fish at a time when there are more than we can handle or market.
Therefore we feel that, by removing the pressure from the fresh fish industry, by regulating the flow of export of our salt fish, we shall assist indirectly but materially the fresh fish business and bring about the prosperity of those engaged in the industry.
For these reasons I believe that the proposition which is now placed before the house is a fair one. It is a modest one, but I believe it will meet the immediate requirements of those whom under the circumstances it is intended to help.

I am sure the house will appreciate the action of the minister in yielding to our requests that he should give us the information which he has just put on the record. Certainly it would 71492-2821
have been unfortunate if we had had to debate the matter with nothing before us but the bill itself, and the somewhat vague resolution. His remarks help us to understand the situation. They were full of information, and appropriate.
Nevertheless, I find some difficulty in reconciling the bill with the resolution on which it is based. The resolution dealt with certain general remedies which it indicated, and also suggested that assistance might be given. In speaking to the resolution the minister stated:
It is intended to provide a limited amount of money to enable the board to carry on its work, and provide some assistance to the fishermen who cannot make enough out of their industry. . . .
And so on. The idea, of course, was to help out the fishermen, who, as we know, are in dire need. It was a worthy picture, and very desirable that we should give this assistance to this class of men who, I am afraid, are trying to hang on to a dead or a dying industry.
One supposed from the remarks made by the minister when the resolution was under discussion that it would apply to all Canada, although the answer he gave to hon. members from Vancouver-North, South, and East, I think-made us doubtful on that point. But the minister assured us that nothing would prevent the possibility of British Columbia- or the Pacific coast, which is the same thing- participating. The bill, however, puts the matter in a somewhat different light. It seems to me that it is a complement, or a supplement-I do not know which you would call it-of an item which has since appeared in the supplementary estimates:
612. To provide for assisting the salt fish branch of the fishing industry, $800,000.
That is reasonably close to a million dollars. Perhaps I am looking at the matter from the wrong point of view, but on the face of it, it looks to me that the purport of the bill is one of straight bonusing of the maritime fishermen by giving them $800,000 this year less the cost of administering the money; and apparently it leaves the Pacific coast out of the picture. When the resolution was before the house the minister said, in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green):
It is not the intention of the government to make this board exclusive in any way. It is not intended to eliminate the possibility of extending the operations of the board to the Pacific coast.
Again, in answer to a further question by the hon. member for Vancouver South-
Is it intended that the act shall apply to the Pacific coast?

-the answer given by the minister was:
The salt fish of the Pacific coast can come under the act; it is not intended to exclude it.
Further on he 6aid:
There is nothing in the bill-
He had the bill in front of him, no doubt; we had not.
-to exclude British Columbia or to prevent it from being represented. There is nothing definite about it, either.
Then the hon. member for Vancouver South asked where these three men constituting the board would come from: would they all come from the maritimes? The minister replied that he did not know. Let us look at the bill itself, page 2. It reads:
The headquarters of the board shall be at the city of Halifax-

Later on, in section 8, it provides for the appointment of an advisory committee or committees. Under these circumstances why not be frank about the matter and say that this is a bill wholly for the advantage-the necessary advantage, I do not question it for a moment-of the maritime fishermen, and that if it succeeds, possibly in another year Pacific coast conditions will be taken in also? But why camouflage it and suggest that there is nothing to hinder us from coming in under it, when we find that the board is to have its headquarters in the city of Halifax? I doubt not that the members also will come from that neighbourhood. I do not want to raise the question of the east against the west; I do not think I have been in the habit of doing that in this house; but it does appear to me to be in line with the whole policy of the fisheries department as at present constituted, not only for this year but for years past.
My mind runs to the annual grant of $160,000 put through under the alleged auspices of chapter 74 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, the title of which is, "An Act to encourage the development of the sea fisheries and the building of fishing vessels." The purpose is to aid the fishing industry of Canada; that is all. I am not leaving out any pregnant part of the act; that is the purpose for which it was passed a number of years ago. Under that act $160,000 is spent on the Atlantic every year in litte useless dribs and drabs here and there, one fisherman getting 18.75, somebody else $11, and so on. That is supposed to encourage the deep-sea fisherman.

But, are there no such fishermen on the Pacific coast? I have brought this question up time and time again in years gone by, but it has always excited so much the ill will of hon. gentlemen from the maritimes, and therefore I abandoned it, their support to the government being more numerous than that from British Columbia. Their argument has always been, "We will do it anyhow." I have never heard any more potent argument put forward than that.

speechtext:
I shall be happy to hear
what the hon. gentleman has to say. I may explain, in courtesy to him, that there was a sum of money granted by the United States, but it was put into the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, and any money that goes into that fund is absolutely lost in the sense that it is no longer earmarked for any specific purpose. It becomes a part of the general funds of Canada. That is a postulate in law with which we are all familiar. Years after that money was put into the consolidated revenue fund-not immediately but years after-the government passed the act to which I have just referred, to encourage the development of the sea fisheries and the building of fishing vessels. I quote:
The governor in council may authorize the payment, out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, of an annual grant not exceeding $160,000, to aid in the development of the sea fisheries of Canada, and the encouragement of the building and fitting out of improved fishing vessels and the improvement of the condition of the fishermen.
That has absolutely no reference to the previous transaction to which the hon. gentleman refers. I know, of course, that is the argument to which they cling. They figure the payment at three per cent, representing

Salt Fish Board
interest on the money paid by the United States; but the only trouble is that is not what happened. The money was not set aside at all for the purpose which hon. members from the maritime provinces suggest. If it had been it would have been indicated in 1874, but it was either in 1878 or 1879 that there was passed the act to which I have alluded. As the money was put into the consolidated revenue fund, I repeat, it lost its identity as much as if one threw a cup of milk into the ocean, and therefore hon. members from the maritime provinces cannot argue that they have any rights in connection with that money. I am sorry I introduced such a belligerent subject, because I know how it affects my hon. friends. The inborn knowledge that they are wrong makes them all the more sore. I remember even the Hon. Mr. Rhodes getting upset, and he was a man of genial temperament. But this is only in line with the policy of "The mari-times first, British Columbia nowhere."
We have seen a grant of $500,000 in recent years included in the estimates for the aid of destitute fishermen, but I do not believe that any of it reached British Columbia. I wish to be fair to the minister. I asked him last year whether any portion of that $500,000 would go to British Columbia, and he said that if the provincial government asked for it they would get their share, but that the province had not done so. I asked what amount would be appropriated for British Columbia in that event and he mentioned the sum of $50,000. Fifty thousand dollars was to be our share out of half a million; yet we provide more than fifty per cent of the fisheries wealth of Canada. Then we find this year this $S00,000, in regard to which British Columbia is again to be very much the unwanted stepchild.
The minister may say, as in fact he did say, that the need of the maritimes is greater than ours. That may be true in a certain degree, but he also said in answer to one of the Vancouver members that our output in dollars of salted fish was something like half a million while that of the maritimes was three millions. Does not that very fact suggest, not that we do not. need attention but that we do need some consideration in this direction to help us to develop an industry which is producing only half a million while the maritime provinces are producing three millions? Owing to the long haul from the Atlantic the sale in British Columbia of maritime salted fish is verv small. It has to come by train, and it is really sold only to a few people who, to gratify a personal taste, can
afford what is almost a luxury, a high-priced article. But if we went into the salt fish business in British Columbia and were given some of the encouragement which this bill indicates will be given on the other side oi the continent, we might build up a trade in a similar class of fish; and as the fish would be produced and processed locally, we could sell it at a price within the reach of people with smaller incomes. In this way a considerable trade could be built up to the advantage of British Columbia-which, by the way, is a part of Canada-and it would take hardly one cent from the industry in the east. In fact, it would be supplementary to and not competitive with that industry.
The minister will no doubt say there is nothing to prevent us from coming under the act. No; on paper there is nothing to prevent us. but we won't. Anyone who reads the bill will agree with me. The board is to be set up at Halifax, and we are 4,000 miles away. Can one imagine this advisory board making representations on our behalf? The men will, of course, be locally appointed. The minister himself said that they must be experts in that particular line of business, and no doubt we shall see men from that part of the country appointed to the board.
These are matters that make British Columbia begin to get a little doubtful whether we are in confederation at all or just outside it. The members from British Columbia are not even allowed to decide among themselves, so to speak, matters with which they are thoroughly familiar from their local knowledge-and our local knowledge must be admitted. We had the humiliating spectacle the other day of being outvoted in the fisheries committee by members from the maritimes who turned up only when there was danger of a vote being taken. Their absence on many other occasions practically precludes th>'- having any intelligent grasp of the situation.
Another objection that I voiced before when the resolution was under discussion-is, why not take in all fish, including fresh fish? I do not know any bill which could so easily lend itself to taking in both branches. The board will have agents trying to drum up this salt fish market; probably they will use the agents of the Department of Trade and Commerce in the countries alluded to, Cuba, the West Indies and so on. Well, if they happened to come across an opportunity-for, after all, when one is calling on people interested in salt fish, it is easy to say a few words on the other side of the industry also-these agents might well be of real value to the maritimes by being able to introduce or influ-

ence business or interest people and find an outlet not only for salt but for fresh fish.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think it would be practicable to export fresh fish to Cuba?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INVESTIGATION OF MARKETING AND ASSISTANCE TO PRODUCERS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
No, absolutely not, but Cuba was not the only place I mentioned. We have trade agents in a great many places, for instance New York. I only instanced that, saying that when such an agent was pushing the sale of salt fish he might readily, having come in contact with fish agents and dealers, find an outlet for some fresh fish as well.
The minister said he was not inclined to go into that aspect because we have produced too many fresh fish already, more than we can readily market. Is that not the purpose of the bill, because we are producing more salt fish also than we can readily market? Here is a point to which I do not think the minister paid attention. There is a trend to-day, and has been for the last few years, away from salt fish to fresh fish. The greater facilities of transportation by fast trains, aeroplanes and the like, and the discovery within recent years of a new method of freezing by which fish can be kept in incomparably better condition than they used to be, all tend to get away from salt fish to the sale of fish in the fresh state, in the same way that there has been a tendency for many years to get away from the horse-drawn vehicle and use the machine. Instead of trying to sweep back the ocean, by putting forward a bill to develop a horse-drawn-car industry so to speak, would it not be better for us to take knowledge of the drift of events, to see that the trend is towards fresh fish, to direct and control it, not ignore it until we find ourselves left out on a limb, but control and direct the trend so that as the change comes bit by bit we shall be able to switch from the salt fish industry as it dies or gets less, into the fresh fish end of the business and so benefit all our fishing industry? For that reason alone the bill should read "fish" instead of "saltfish" alone. I am not asking this for British Columbia alone, it might be of real benefit to the development and increase of the fresh fish industry of the maritimes.
To come to the bill itself, the resolution said that the purpose was to give assistance to producers of salt fish for export. I emphasize that, "producers of salt fish." But if one reads the bill itself, does it say "producers"? Not a bit, it says "exporters." Section 6 states that the board may give assistance to "exporters" of fish. Not to producers. The 
resolution said "producers," and it is the producers we are interested in, is it not? But the bill itself is confined entirely to exporters of fish. An hon. gentleman behind me says it is a printer's error, but it is repeated twice in the same section.
