speechtext:
We find the Nova Scotia trawlers given preference, the British Columbia trap owners given preference, and now the maritime exporters are to be the centre of the picture, but not the producer. The resolution said "producer," but now it is not the producer, it is the exporter. I wonder what my hon. friends from the prairies would say if we had given a bonus on wheat but confined it entirely to the middlemen, the elevator companies, instead of the producer. And no matter what my hon. friend behind me may say, there is only one meaning of the word " producer," that is the man who produces the wheat or fish as the case may be.
The way I read this-I may be wrong- is that the purpose of the bill is to give a bonus of 25 per cent to the salt fish exporters; the exporters only. Mention is made of other lines of investigation, but it is evident that the outstanding feature is the 25 per cent bonus, especially in this year of jubilee, otherwise an election. The minister might well argue that he is not alone in this policy of bonusing. It is true; we have gone on a bonusing spree. It is like a man taking opium or some opium derivative, it puts him in a fine, happy condition for the time being, but by and by he needs another shot, soon an increased dose, and so it goes. The bonus

Salt Fish Board
system is something the same, but it has one additional worse feature. The dope fiend exhibits a dreadful example and warning to his neighbours; but in the case of the bonus it is the other way about, it has a seductive note. When an individual or an industry or a class has been getting a bonus without working for it, the neighbouring class or perhaps some other industry says, " Me too! Why can we not have a bonus also?"
The opponents of this government brand it as a " do-nothing " government. I do not share that view, I think they have done many worth while things. But they might well be described as a " bonusing " government, although I admit that bonusing was not unknown to the previous government, and its increase is probably due to the natural increase in demand rather than the fact or perhaps as well to the fact that there is an election coming on.
Conditions in the maritimes have been bad for years, so why is it only now discovered what the trouble is and what the remedy should be? We bonus many things; we bonus coal, the coal movement in my district is bonused; we bonus wheat, butter, cheese, and now we are going to bonus the fish industry or part of it. We have bonused the manufacturers by means of the tariff, and there are other bonuses that I have forgotten. Bonusing is getting to be so common in the world now that all nations are probably forced to it, in the same way that Great Britain, having built up a great nation on free trade, had to abandon it simply because of the pressure of the whole world erecting tariffs. Bonusing is a fairly easy although only a temporary solution of any problem caused by the loss of markets, and in an election year it is calculated to be popular for the moment. But it bears some relation, and a fairly close one, to keeping people on relief. To devise a real and permanent solution is a much longer and harder problem, for both the minister charged with formulating the policy, the officials who have to carry it out and the people who have to be trained in new and better methods of production and processing, and possibly, in some instances, required to remove themselves into some other line of activity. But that is the only permanent method. Bonusing is an easier way; getting something for nothing will make them happy for a little time. But then comes the day when they want more. Next year they will want more bonus, and so on. Once they have tasted the rich gravy of a bonus, there will be a persistent demand for the maintenance and increase of that flow of easy money, and the cold shoulder will be turned on the harder
methods of finding different forms of marketing and adapting oneself to different methods of producing, processing and so on.
I have before me a well prepared article, upon which I congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), written by Mr. W. F. Fraser, Canadian trade commissioner, on conditions in Jamaica. A great many of these reports contain just a few generalities and figures one can get out of the year book, but this report is chock-full of useful and valuable information. I understand that Jamaica is a crown colony; the government have established a marketing division. They operate a refrigerator unit where they box and ship on behalf of the growers a large variety of tropical fruits and vegetables. Originally this was an experiment, but it has been so highly successful that it is being made a distinct branch of the government. Further on, it is said that they are going to establish a plant for the production of dried milk, and they are taking steps to provide that the government will be able to fix by law not only wholesale and retail prices for the product but also the prices to be paid by the factory to the dairymen. That smacks of the soviet idea, yet this is good old Britain. I mention this only as an illustration of a better policy for us to adopt than simply to hand these men a bonus of a few dollars for the time being.
Let us now look at the machinery under the bill itself. This is to be just another board or commission, and it seems to me, speaking subject to correction, that this is the fifth board or commission we have set up this year. I would suggest that for every two commissions or boards we appoint, the government should be required to cut out one cabinet post, with the idea that there will be less work for the cabinet to do with these boards and commissions in operation. Pretty soon we are going to have commissions running Canada; they are running a great deal of it now. I am always against commissions and boards if they are divorced or separated from government responsibility. I would have no objection to leaving the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) in charge of this matter; then he would be responsible to parliament. But when, in connection with railway matters and many others, we ask a minister for some information, he is in a position to say, "I am sorry, but this is run by a commission. All I can do is pass on your remarks and if the commission feel like answering they will do so." I do not like that system.
Let me refer to sections 3 and 4 of the bill. How familiar it all sounds; how often we have
Salt Fish Board
COMMONb
heard it. It is provided that there shall be a board, to be known as the salt fish board, to consist of three members appointed by the governor in council, one of whom shall be chairman, another will be vice-chairman and the third will be the audience. Each member shall hold office during pleasure; they are not to be appointed by the civil service commission; their salaries will be fixed by the governor in council; two members of the board will form a quorum; the headquarters shall be in the city of Halifax, and of course they will have power, with the approval of the governor in council, to employ such technical or other officers, clerks and employees as may be necessary. This is another good opportunity for giving political preferment to friends. Here is another department to be built up round this board or commission. As I said before, you give a man a job and right away he wants somebody to help him do it.
We must remember that this is all to be for the salt fish end of the industry only; they are forbidden to touch the fresh fish industry at all. It is easy to knock, and I believe the man who knocks should be in a position to suggest something in place of what he complains about. This is what I suggest: Have your board, certainly, but have it located at Ottawa. Let it be composed of permanent officials already under salary, one representing the fisheries department, one representing the trade and commerce department and the third representing the finance department. It will not cost anything for their salaries, and they will be able to find time to attend to this work. It will not cost anything for stenographic or clerical assistance, because already we have plenty of officials to do the work. It will not cost anything for rent, light or fuel. It will be found that in Halifax they will be building or renting offices to accommodate this board. Then appoint your advisory committees. The bill provides that such advisory committees shall be paid their travelling expenses, but no salaries. I agree with that, but let me suggest that they be paid only their reasonable travelling and living expenses. Let there be none of this nonsense of paying a man $20 a day for living expenses, and having him come on the platform boasting of what he was doing for the good of the country and the love of God, without salary, when actually he was receiving $20 a day or over $7,000 a year, more than he would ever get in his life at any other occupation. Do not do that. If your practical men are not sufficiently interested to give their advice without receiving more than their travelling and living expenses, they are not very much 
use. Let there be a central board here, with one committee in Halifax and another in Vancouver. The cost would be very small, and I believe the work would be well done.
The bill provides that the advisory committees shall consist of five members, two of whom shall represent the fishermen-producers, and three, the dealers or exporters. Do it the other way round; have at least three producers and only two dealers or exporters. Believe me, the dealers have enough connections with which to take care of themselves; do not worry about that. These committees could do good work. For instance, with a treaty under negotiation or the adjustment of a treaty coming up, they would be able to give useful, valuable information. Perhaps, if there had been local advisory committees before the treaty was negotiated with the United States we would not be in such a muddle in connection with vegetable oils, because they could have given the necessary information in time to have had the matter adjusted. Let us have the board run from Ottawa, and as I said before, let us include fresh fish. No one would be injured, certainly not the maritimes, and both coasts might receive material benefits. It would be far cheaper and would do away with any tendency to build up another department round this board.
I hesitate to vote against this bill. I will not vote against it, because it promises immediate aid to these fishermen who, as we all know, are in unfortunate circumstances. But it will involve a large expenditure and very unnecessary official machinery, and seems to hold no promise of permanent improvement in the lot of the fishermen except to encourage them to look to another year in the hope of getting a bigger and better bonus, which I believe is calculated to undermine their morale rather than to encourage them to go on and try to help themselves. To test the point with regard to fresh fish when we are in committee, I propose to move that the word "salt" be struck out, so that both the title and purpose of the bill will cover fresh as well as salt fish throughout the dominion.

I shall not take time to discuss the sections, but would point out that, generally speaking, the bill will give assistance to fishermen and enaible them to compete in foreign markets.
As I understand this legislation, it is breaking new ground so far as federal legislation is concerned. It is a measure taken to ensure Canadian fisheries a position in the salt fish markets of the world. We are now taking cognizance of world changes which have, been gradually straining free commerce and trade among countries. That free exchange of products which in former years used to take place has now become impossible because of various countries endeavouring by means of bounties and subsidies to push their exports into other countries.
I believe one cannot fully appreciate the effect of a bill without considering briefly the development of the salt fish industry in the maritime provinces. It must be remembered that the salting of ground fish, in particular, was Canada's first industry, and that no branch of employment has engaged our people for as long a period. The first inhabitants who came to our shores settled on the land for the purpose of salting fish. The development of the industry can be divided briefly into four periods, the first of which extended from 1497 until about 1600 when people from the old country carried the products of our coastal waters back to Europe. The second period extended from about 1600 to about 1732 when the French and English settled on the lands adjoining the Atlantic coast for the purpose of drying their fish. During that time markets in Portugal, Spain and the West Indies were developed. From 1732 until about 1920 there was a rise and fall in the salt fish industry. From 1920 until the present time we have found ourselves in a rather vicious circle, when countries have been trying to gain access to markets they lost during the war, and have made intensive efforts to capture markets which previously we had held.
I have before me some figures of production in Nova Scotia in the second and last periods.
I have the figures in five-year periods and, without going into too much detail, I shall

refer to a few of them. In 1869 our production stood at 464,000 hundredweight. That production gradually increased until about 1886, when we were producing 791,000 hundredweight.

What was the value?
Mr. POl TIER: I have not those figures, but I would say they would be worth about $4 or So per quintal. However, I am not sure as to the exact amount. Production gradually decreased until about 1936, when we were producing in Nova Scotia 117,000 hundredweight, or about one-sixth of the peak production in former years. The Canadian production of dried cod in 1889 was
896,000	hundredweight, and by 1937 this had dropped to 296,000 hundredweight. There was a gradual decrease as the years went by. The reasons for the increase in production up to 1888 were: first, the inauguration by the dominion government of a protection fleet which prevented United States vessels from fishing in Canadian territorial waters in the period 1870-1872; second, lack of employment in other industries in the period 1873-1879; third, the payment of a bounty to fishermen authorized under an act passed in 1882 and, fourth, the accessibility of such markets as the British and Spanish West Indies and the United States.
The reasons for the decline which occurred after 1886 were: first, the change in the method of transportation from sailing vessel to steamer; second, the rise of the sugar beet industry in Europe which seriously affected the West Indies trade in cane sugar, thereby lessening the purchasing power of those islands; third, the effectiveness of tariffs in foreign countries against fish; fourth, due to the boom in construction which took place in the New England states, larger numbers of our people went to that part of the country; fifth, there was also the loss of a considerable part of the domestic market for dried cod on account of the improvement in refrigerating methods and processing which made fresh fish more readily available to our own markets; sixth, there was the effectiveness of competition from the salt cod industries of foreign countries. This last reason for the decline began to be evident about 1922, and this competition has been more intensive since then. When the minister introduced the bill a few days ago he referred to this period, and I agree with the remark he made at that time with regard to the foreign competition.
Because of the different causes for the decline in production to which I have referred,

the self-contained fishing communities which used to be found all along the shores of the maritime provinces are disappearing. The back-bone, so to speak, of the fishing industry has gradually disappeared, and as a result we have the conditions that are present to-day. Two things occurred when this decline in production took place. The people were forced to find something to do in order to eat and carry on. Many of them went into the fresh fish industry, and further, lobster fishing was developed in a number of districts. Unfortunately, the equipment necessary to carry on lobster fishing is more costly than that necessary in ground fishing.
To bring the picture to my own constituency, the production of dried cod in Yarmouth county in 1871 was 96,8il quintals; 'by 1891 this had decreased to 34,729 hundredweight, and by 1931 there was no production at all. This is perhaps an extreme example of the trend in the dried codfish industry, but it shows what is happening all along the line. The production in Shelburne county in 1871 was 48,835 quintals; by 1881 this had increased to 128,949 quintals, but by 1931 the production had dropped to 2,15b nundredweight. In Digby County from 16.227 quintals to 469 hundredweight. Unfortunately, as this decline in production occurred, the salt fish industry in Nova Scotia centred in two areas. This had a double effect upon the outlying districts which were dependent upon this type of fishing. The two districts in which the salt fish industry settled are Lunenburg and Halifax. I do not criticize the people of these districts at all for endeavouring to gather round themselves that part of the salt fish industry which still remained.
Even when one looks at the declining process he cannot see the whole picture in so far as the outlying parts of the province are concerned. Perhaps I am trying the patience of the house when I repeat myself, but I want to make it quite clear that two things happened. The decline in the salt fish industry was approximately from five to one, and what was left of the industry centred in two areas. It can easily be seen what effect this had upon the people in the outlying districts who were dependent upon this type of fishing. They suffered greatly. I shall be glad to look into the matter. Could the hon. member advise me approximately when the dismissal occurred?
I can give that information to the minister. I have some letters.

I shall 'be glad to get it. With regard to the suggestion of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid),
I understand that the boxes are purchased by tender. I shall, however, look into the matter and see whether they can be more economically obtained.
Tinsmiths and others in British Columbia have informed me that they would be pleased to supply the boxes at half the present cost.
I notice in the details on page 160 of the estimates that three draftsmen are mentioned as being employed by the department. What do they do?
They are engaged in drafting in connection with mechanical equipment used in the city post offices, and in the preparation of post office maps.

For some years I have
suggested to previous Postmasters General that there should be something of a businesslike statement from this department. We seem to be going through the estimates this year in the same old way without any conception of what the annual revenues and expenditures are. I have not yet had an opportunity to go through these estimates carefully, but I suggest that both for the sake of the post office and in order that we may have an intelligent understanding of the working of the department the minister should explain the operations of this branch of government in the last year from the point of view of revenues and expenditures. The committee would in that way obtain a better idea of the true state of affairs than by taking the estimates item by item as we have done in the past.
Mr. McLARTY': For some years I have heard the hon. member suggest that the Post Office Department might with advantage prepare a statement which would more nearly coincide with that prepared by the ordinary public or private utility. Sitting in a place which was perhaps less prominent but often more comfortable, I thought his suggestion was quite reasonable and fair, and the question I had in mind when first appointed as
Postmaster General was how far we could go along that line, being anxious indeed to comply with the request that had been made. But I found this difficulty. If one endeavoured to analyse operations into an effective balance sheet there would be so much approximation that its value as a balance sheet would be largely lost. Let me give two illustrations of the difficulty with which we are confronted. Take the matter of the postage stamps used on cheques in lieu of excise stamps. Some years ago, when the excise tax was first imposed, excise stamps were required to be put on cheques and postage stamps could not be used. This, however, was found to be a definite inconvenience to the public, and consequently the regulations were altered to permit of the alternative use of postage stamps. I have discussed the matter with various officials of the department, and I find that there is no practical way, without public inconvenience, of determining the exact amount of revenue which the postal service receives as a result of the use of postage stamps on cheques.
Could it not be done by embossing the cheques themselves?

That is done, elsewhere,
I believe, but in view of the varying amount of stamps required on cheques in Canada that method would not afford a complete answer.
They do it in Great Britain.

I believe there is a
uniform tax rate on cheques in Great Britain. We have a graduated scale.
Take, again, the question of rentals. The Post Office Department does not pay rentals to the government or to the public works department on buildings which are occupied by the Post Office Department. The question might readily arise as to the appropriate rental which it should pay on the buildings occupied. As the committee knows, post offices throughout Canada, federal buildings, have been built not only for the utilitarian purpose which they serve as a medium for the department to conduct its business, but also to gratify the natural civic pride of the communities in which they are situated. Should the post office fix a rental based upon an investment where the building is more elaborate than it need be for postal services, or should it pay a rental based simply upon the appropriate amount required in order to afford adequate postal facilities?
I give these two illustrations to point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North that any balance sheet would be an approximation.
Supply-Post Office

Without, however, putting it in the form of a balance sheet, we have the estimates on various matters except the amount which the post office obtains in the way of excise on cheques, which we cannot possibly obtain without inconvenience to the public, and we should be glad to give any figures or departmental estimate of what these amounts are.
I do not say it would be impossible, but I am afraid it would be very costly. For example, I went into the question of how this is calculated in the United States. There, I believe, they have a most thorough analysis of postal revenues. They have a cost ascertainment commission which works thoroughly. A subdivision is made, and one can get practically any estimation that is required. But the difficulty is the cost. The staff work required to be done by that commission to obtain its report costs, I am advised, in excess of SI ,000,000. I am not suggesting that we cannot do the same thing in Canada, that we cannot comply with the request which the hon. member has made so often; but I suggest that it might be a question whether the balance sheet when obtained would be worth the cost of preparing it. For the benefit of the hon. member however, if there is any figure which we can put in the balance sheet, subject to the explanation that it is only approximate and only an estimate, I should be only too glad to give it to him.

I am not at all anxious to have the department incur the expense of preparing what might be considered a perfect balance sheet, but I do desire to have some approximation to show the state of affairs in the department. The two illustrations which the minister has given are not altogether a satisfactory explanation. He speaks of rentals on buildings occupied for postal purposes. I fully realize that sometimes post office buildings are put up where they are not really required, and in communities where they were never called for by the department. I realize further that post office buildings are often made more ornamental than buildings used for ordinary commercial purposes, but we can allow for that in any balance sheet brought down to show the workings of the department. On the other hand, as regards stamps used on cheques to-day, which are shown as revenue to the Post Office Department, we can get an approximation. We can get an approximation, for instance, if we take the last year in which revenue stamps were placed in post offices; that would give some idea of the amount, and we could take that as the best authority we could get. What the amount was I do not know, but I think it could be

easily ascertained from the Department of Finance for the last year in which we issued excise stamps to place on cheques. But even if we did not go further in that regard, what I should like to know is what the post office revenue is for a year, what the operations cost for a year, and then strike a reasonable balance sheet to show whether during that period the post office paid its way or whether there was a loss.
So far as rentals of buildings are concerned, I think the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) a year or two ago made out some scale of rentals which he said could be charged to the Post Office Department. There is no reason why a utility like the post office should not be run, to a certain extent at any rate, the same as any other utility operated by a public body, and have an approximate balance sheet at the end of the year.

The revenue for the fiscal year 1937-38 was 842,998,000. I omit the hundreds. The revenue for the fiscal year 1938-39 was $43,130,000. The net revenue was $35,546,000 for the year 1937-38, and for the year 1938-39 it was estimated at S35,535,000. If you give the figure on the basis that has been heretofore shown in the annual report of the Post Office Department it would show a total excess of revenue over expenditures of approximately $1,300,000. If you break that down on the basis on which the estimates were broken down two years ago when the post office estimates, instead of being divided into civil government and outside service of the post office, in other words charging the headquarters to the Post Office Department, which was not done until the estimates of last year, on that basis a surplus of $99,618 is left. That does not include rentals. The approximate figure for rentals, subject to the remarks I have previously made, is, according to post office officials, $3,077,300. Then, if you charge against that the value of franking privileges, the estimated expense of operating post office savings banks, the estimated cost of free conveyance, of newspapers, the estimated postage value of franked provincial government documents, the estimated postal value of literature for the blind, you have an offsetting item of $1,090,600.
I do not think I can be any more definite than that, unless the hon. member has something specific in mind.
In the item of revenue I suppose the minister includes the revenue from stamps used for placing on cheques.

Yes, we include that in our revenue.

Supply-Post Office

In addition to the items of expenditure which the Postmaster General has given to the committee, there might well be included fuel which is purchased through the public works department, and also certain supplies and equipment which are provided for in the estimates of the public works department.

I am told that is all
included, both coal and equipment, in the rental figures estimated as I say as to what would be appropriately payable if the post office were standing on its own feet.

Perhaps it is in the figures the minister has given, but I point out that these are purchased and paid for out of the estimates of other departments than the post office.
There are very few items in the estimates of the Post Office Department. I should like to ask the minister one or two questions, and I am sure that even if they may not be strictly appropriate under this item, he will be pleased to give us the information.
There was a recent reduction of 50 per cent in the charges for special delivery of letters. What is the revenue derived from that source? Of course that revenue is entirely derived from services in towns and cities; I do not believe we have any special delivery in rural districts. It occurred to me that this service is very valuable, one for which those receiving the service should be willing to pay the small amount that was charged. What led to the reduction being made? Is it the idea that a larger number of letters would be sent by special delivery if the charge were cut in half, and so additional revenue received? It would appear to me that if a reduction could have been made in the general rate of postage rather than for special delivery service, which is available only for towns and cities, it would be much more in the interest of the public.

The purpose of the reduction in the charge for special delivery letters was, as the hon. member suggests, to bring about an increase in business. I regret I have not before me the figures to show the remarkable increase that followed on the reduction. I believe, speaking from recollection, the increase in various cities ran from 65 per cent to 187 per cent. There was a definite increase. I do not suggest that this is entirely as a result of the reduction in the charge, because at about the same time there was an increased use of air mail special delivery service.
The figures for special delivery can hardly be fairly compared with what would happen
in case of a reduction in the general postage rate. The figures are rather small-
There is, I fancy, a wide spread between them.

For instance, for the year ending March, 1938, sales of special delivery stamps were approximately $38,508. I think my hon. friend will realize that the comparison would be a little far-fetched. What we are trying to do, however, is to improve the special delivery service, and we are taking steps to do that and to broaden its use as far as possible.

First I should like to congratulate the new minister upon his appointment to this high office. The post office comes in contact with the public more perhaps than any other department, and we need at the head of this department a man with the human touch and personality that characterize the present head.
I have had correspondence from all the universities of Canada and all the great libraries regarding a resolution which I had on the order paper concerning the reduction of postal rates on library books. I wish to thank the minister for carrying out the proposals which have been made for many years by the libraries and the universities to lower the postal rates on books so that the public could get books from the libraries through the mails at a cheaper rate. I should not like to read all the letters I have received; they might make the minister think he is the all-important personage in the cabinet, but I have received many congratulatory messages from heads of universities and others, and as a humble member of the House of Commons I feel quite honoured to receive these letters from such eminent persons of such high educational standing in Canada, who recognize that the Postmaster General has done something for the reading public.
It is well known that if our people are to understand and make use of the new knowledge that is available in the world to-day they must be able to read about and understand the problems facing them. Books have greatly enlarged our horizons and given us a new field of joy truly marvellous in its richness. In imagination humanity can now reach out and travel the world over; through science we can obtain glimpses of knowledge hitherto unknown. I am not going to deliver a speech on this subject; I do not suppose the minister would like me to do so, but I should like to say a few words at this time because I feel that the service which has been rendered in this way should be recognized by all members
Supply-Post Office

of the house, irrespective of party, because human knowledge must go on.
When Rowland Hill first introduced the idea of penny postage into the British House of Commons it was treated as a joke, but it has become an enormous success. The progress of reform has gone on when people have seen what was wrong and been determined to set the wrong right. People thought penny postage a joke because it would not be profitable and therefore would be a bad thing for the government, but they found that through the reduction in postal rates much greater use was made of the post office, and consequently a better understanding was developed throughout Britain. If democracy is to live, the masses of poor and, in many instances, ignorant people at the bottom of society must have an opportunity to have the best that is in them trained and strengthened, so that they may worthily take their place in this wonderful world. In this day and age it is a disgrace for anyone to grow up in ignorance; and while we strive to provide better schools, commodious public libraries, museums, beautiful picture galleries and cheap books, we should also strive to place a knowledge of these things in the hands of our people. Step by step more and more people have gained the right to share the government; step by step more and more people have come to read good books as they have been made available. We cannot develop democracy without education, and if we expect our people to govern themselves we cannot keep them eternally ignorant. So I think this departure under the new minister, in the lowering of postal rates on library books, deserves the commendation of every member of this House of Commons; and on behalf of the universities of Canada, those in charge of the various public libraries and the library societies of every province, the schools, teachers and all those in any way affected by this change, I sincerely congratulate the minister and trust that more and more people will take advantage of this opportunity which has been made available by the Postmaster General.

I appreciate very much the kindly commendation of the hon. member for Vegreville. Might I suggest, since there is so much glory going round, that some should be reflected on the hon. member, in view of his honest and sincere efforts to obtain this reduction.

When the minister was estimating the cost of the postal service, he referred to the fact that the Post Office Department did not pay rent to the Depart-

ment of Public Works for government buildings used as post offices. In that connection I should like to ask the minister whether the Post Office Department pays for the lighting, heating and caretaking of such buildings or whether the Department of Public Works meets these expenses as well; and also whether that would be taken into account in estimating the cost of the postal service.
The post office does not pay public works for these services, but in the round amount of rentals which is estimated in the previous figures the cost of these services is calculated.

I should like to associate myself with what was said by the hon. member for Vegreville. I was approached in this connection by a number of teachers' organizations across the country, and although I have not received any eulogistic letters of thanks to pass on to the minister, I took the opportunity of expressing my thanks to him in person not so long ago. I believe this service rendered by the post office will be deeply appreciated by all classes of our citizens who can avail themselves of it, and particularly on behalf of the teachers who have approached me during the past few months I want to join my hon. friend in expressing my appreciation of this change.
I thank the hon. member.
What is the situation with regard to postage meters? I understand the government grants a licence for the whole of Canada-
I might suggest to my hon. friend that this would come under the next item. I do not want to restrict discussion in any way, but his question properly comes under that item.

Item agreed to.
276. Post offices, including salaries and other expenses of headquarters and staff post offices and supplies and equipment for revenue post offices, $15,484,810.

I should like an explanation of the operation of the postage meter machines. I believe one company has a licence for the whole of Canada; that this company is the Canadian subsidiary of a United States company, and that it rents out these machines to individuals. I understand also that the business is growing all the time and in due course will become a very big business. It does seem that we are allowing a vested interest to grow up in connection with a public service.

Supply-Post Office

The Post Office Department does not sell or rent the metered machines. Any company that makes such machines which will meet with the approval of the Post Office Department can rent their machines to any company approved by the Post Office Department. In other words, the Post Office Department merely approves the particular machine, and it will approve any machine that comes up to its standard. It is not a case of one company enjoying any monopoly.

Is it not a fact that at the present time only one machine has been approved, namely that manufactured by the Canadian Postage Meters and Machines Company Limited, which, as I have said, is really just a subsidiary of a United States company? Why cannot Canada carry on that business herself?

I believe it is a fact that only one company is now supplying meters, and that only one company has submitted machines for approval. It is a world-wide company which sells meters not only in Canada and the United States but in Great Britain, Germany and other countries.
Is that the way in which the meter or stamp-vending machine is handled in Great Britain? I refer to the machine that is seen in stores and other public places.
I am advised it is handled in exactly the same way.
The machines have the words " post office " right on them.
In Canada and in Great Britain postage meters are purely a rental proposition.
I am surprised to hear that.
Is there any possibility of the government doing that business itself?
I imagine that to go into the manufacture of those machines would be a wide extension of the powers of a department, the fundamental purpose of which is to sell postage stamps and transport mail.
Does the minister know how many machines are in use in Canada?
I am afraid I have not that information, but I shall be pleased to obtain it for the hon. member.

Does the minister imply that the stamp-vending machines found
over post office boxes in the old country are not in the possession of the Post Office Department?
I was referring to the postage meter machines which are rented in the same manner here as they are in the old country. That was my answer.
I was referring to the stamp-vending machines.
I am advised that the Post Office Department has nothing to do with stamp-vending machines.

On a holiday, such as to-day, with the exception of making a purchase in hotels where can a person buy a postage stamp? The branch post offices are closed. I went to one to-day and found that I could not buy a stamp. But in Great Britain stamp-vending machines are found on all prominent corners, and whether or not it is a holiday, a person desiring to buy a stamp puts the necessary amount in the machine and receives his stamp. I have tried it on many occasions. Do I understand the minister to say that in the old country these stamp-vending machines are not under the control of the Post Office Department?

We have none of the street stamp-vending machines in Canada if it is to them that the hon. member is referring. I understand that at one time they were tried in Toronto, with rather unfortunate results. The Post Office Department have none of them in Canada to-day.
Why were they unsuccessful in Toronto?
Because of climatic conditions, and the slugs put into the machines.
The minister understands that I was referring to the postage meter machine?
Yes, and I gave my answer on that understanding.

Perhaps this would be
an appropriate place to ask a question I have in mind in connection with the origin of demands for post offices. For instance, some time ago prominent articles appeared in the newspapers with respect to Tweed, Ontario. Apparently they do not want a new post office in Tweed, and yet it has been foisted upon them. Where does the demand for a post office originate?

The construction of post
offices is purely a matter for the Department of Public Works. In the event of the con-
Supply-Post Office

struction of a public building, the Post Office Department advises the Department of Public Works as to the amount of space which will be required for postal services in the new building. But fortunately the Post Office Department does not have to worry about the purchase of any land or the construction of any building.

But surely that ought
to come under the Postmaster General. We know he has been having considerable trouble in connection with the building at Tweed, and that may be only one of a score. If one looks at the estimates he will see provision for the building of one hundred or two hundred new post office buildings throughout Canada. I am anxious to find out who makes the demand for these buildings.

The buildings so often
referred to as post offices very often contain other departments of government as well. I can assure the hon. member we have nothing to do with the construction or the erection of post offices or the purchase of land or sites which, I understand, is the basis of the controversy which has been widespread in connection with Tweed.
In the event of the Post Office Department not wanting a new post office, do they have to take it?
Not so far as this department is concerned.

Does the Department of
Public Works create a post office building and hand it over to the Post Office Department?

If postal facilities are not available we would unquestionably make a recommendation to the Department of Public Works stating that we require space. But so far as the construction of the building, or anything of that kind is concerned, that is entirely under the control of the Department of Public Works.
May I put it more definitely: Does the Department of Public Works erect in any community a post office which has not been requested by the Post Office Department?

I think it does, because
of the fact that other departments may require housing more than the Post Office Department. Consequently, if a public building is to be erected under those circumstances it would be normal to house the post office in it.

Does the Department of
Public Works make inquiries from the Post Office Department as to whether or not they require facilities in a certain area? This matter has been discussed in the house, and I dislike going over it again. I thought the matter had been adjusted.

Necessarily there must
be a certain amount of cooperation between the departments. I do not know that I can give the hon. member a sufficiently definite answer. I know of several instances where the Department of Public Works have advised us that a federal building was being constructed and have asked what space we would require. On the other hand, if we feel that we require additonal postal facilities we would make the necessary recommendation to the Department of Public Works. I do not think there is the definite dividing line the hon. member has in mind.

It is true that there may be no definite dividing line, but I have the impression that there is not a definite cooperation between the Department of Public Works and the Post Office Department, so far as the erection of public buildings is concerned. I speak with a definite thought in my mind on the point. What I wish to say is that when it comes to a question of erecting a post office, only one department should have the say, and that department should be the one headed by the Postmaster General-not the Department of Public Works. I am trying to help the minister, and not to put any obstacle in his way. I know hon. members who may want some sort of monument in their respective districts will go round to the Department of Public Works and have something erected. As a result the department may erect a building for postal and other facilities which may not be required. Sometimes those buildings are not required, but they give to members or other persons a certain amount of pleasure. In many instances those buildings are only white elephants, so far as the department is concerned.
A few moments ago the minister gave the committee figures showing rentals being paid by the Post Office Department. I believe the figure he gave was a staggering amount, well over $3,000,000, or about ten per cent of the total revenue of the department. That is a fairly high figure. But what I do wish to see is a measure of cooperation between the Department of Public Works and the Post Office Department. There should be a clear and definite understanding that no building will be erected in so far as the Post Office

Supply-Post Office
Department is concerned until that department has given full approval and there is a definite requirement for postal facilities in the area.

The Postmaster General is very genial this evening, and I am sure if he continues in that mood he will get his estimates through rapidly. In the case of Tweed, was it the Post Office Department or the public works department that got into trouble there in connection with the site and building?

I am afraid I shall have to look that up. I cannot say offhand whether we did or did not recommend improved postal facilities. There are a number of instances where they initiated the matter, and there are other instances where we initiated the matter, but I cannot say at the present time into which category Tweed would fall.

I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. McLarty) something which may seem to be trivial, but which is really of great importance to the people in a certain community in my district. This has to do with the mutilation of the name of a post office which has been in existence for over forty years. The name is Whonnock, which is the name of an Indian reservation in that locality. According to a memorandum which I received, the department took upon itself on March 9 last to change the name to Whonock, with one "n." This changes altogether the Indian meaning of the word. A short time ago I received a petition signed by, I believe, about 100 per cent of the residents in this district protesting against this change and urging that the old name be used. I presented this petition to the department, and have received certain reasons for this change. The last one is that no objection was raised. How could the people make any objection when they did not know anything about the matter until the change was made? Another reason given was that representations had been received, I believe from the surveyor general of British Columbia, to the effect that the legal spelling of the name was Whonock. It was also said that the geographic board had something to do with the change. I think anyone who has lived in a community for a number of years will agree that the residents should have something to say about the name of the community. For instance, the district in which I reside is called Chilliwack, an Indian name. The spelling used by the municipality, which is the spelling that was used in the early days, is Chilliwhack. When the city was incorporated some ten or fifteen years ago, the people saw fit to leave out the "h" in the spelling, and it is Chilliwack. They would resent the changing of that name by this or any other department of government.
I am sure if the department decided to take one "t" from the spelling of Ottawa there would be considerable trouble. Another reason given for this change was that the railroad company had taken out one "n" in spelling the name of their station. What a private corporation does should have nothing to do with the matter. The railroad is looking for business from that community, and it is up to them to judge whether it was wise to make that change. I know that the community resent it.
So far as the legal angle is concerned, it is stated that in the brief submitted to the Rowell commission the name was spelled with one "n." I got in touch with the director of Indian affairs to-day, and he told me that the name of this particular reserve has been spelled with two "n's" as far back as the history of the Indian department in British Columbia goes. As I said at the beginning, this matter may be considered trivial, but it is not trivial to these people.
In the petition presented by these people they protested against the action of the Post Office Department in changing the name from Whonnock to Whonock, claiming that it was neither necessary nor correct. They respectfully ask that the Post Office Department be instructed to retain the original Indian name with the two "n's." I just want to leave this with the minister. I have already presented the case, I think quite fully, to the officials of his department, but so far no action has been taken.

I understand the officials of the department acted largely on the representations of the geographic board and the surveyor general. I shall, however, endeavour to make a study of Indian nomenclature and then give consideration to the matter.
I want to impress upon the minister that this matter is considered very important by the people in the district.
I do not wish to make light of it.

I do not think the geographic board or any other of these officials should step in in that way. I am sure there would be considerable protest if the name of Ottawa, or of some other community which
Supply-Post Office

had been in existence for forty or fifty years, were changed. It is my opinion that the Post Office Department should take the advice of the people in the community in which the particular office is situated.

No doubt the Postmaster General is aware that on the recommendation of the acting postmaster general there was placed in the estimates of the public works department last year an item for the purchase of a building at Sintaluta, Saskatchewan, for post office purposes. The building which they had in mind was a former bank building, and I think the amount in the estimates was $3,500. It would have been a splendid buy so far as the department was concerned. I should like to know if the purchase has been completed or, if not, the reason for the delay.
The purchase of a building would be under the public works department.
Would the minister give the matter his attention?
I shall be glad to.

In connection with the observations of the hon member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber), I should like to know whether the Post Office Department takes its cue from the surveying departments of the various provinces. I do know that the cartographers branch in British Columbia has for some years been correcting the names of places throughout the province and as far as possible preventing any duplication. It has been encouraging the use of original native words and spellings where this can conveniently be done. Is any understanding maintained between the survey departments of the provinces and the post office for these purposes?

I believe that the Post Office Department, before making any change of name, endeavours to obtain not only information from the geographic board and the surveys branch, but all other information available.

I wish particularly to thank the department for the change in name they made in a very small postal division in the Yukon. The name was mentioned as the pronunciation called for, but it was not spelled correctly; and upon representations, the department very kindly spelled the name correctly.
I notice on page 161 of the estimates that apparently we have only one postmaster, grade 10. In what city is that postmaster?
In the city of Hamilton.
Has an appointment been made of postmaster at Toronto?
In Toronto the district director is also postmaster, the post office being grade 12.

That is a new grade,
then. On page 161 there is not any grade 12 office mentioned.
It comes under the district director and inspection service.

Before the item is passed, I wish to put in a word for the smaller salaried employees. There are men working in the Post Office Department who get as little as $60 a month. I know of one married man in that situation, and I think we all realize that no married man can live in the city of Ottawa on $60 a month. The man I have in mind has been on the temporary staff for eight years, and if he does not get a permanent appointment within two months he will be out of a position. Possibly I should be blaming the civil service commission, because I understand that civil service regulations govern these matters. I am not finding any fault with higher salaried employees of the Post Office Department, because I believe that the department is run better than, or at any rate as well as, any other department of the government. I hope the present minister will be able to do something to help these low salaried employees.
It is the civil service commission that sets the salaries for the employees of the Post Office Department.
I should like to ask about the mail service on St. Clair avenue, Toronto. May I inquire under this item?
Yes.

The minister has had a letter on the subject from the St. Clair Avenue Business Men's Association, which is made up of business men from, I believe, where Bathurst street crosses St. Clair, to as far west as Silverthorn avenue, a distance of about two miles. These business men represent a district which has become one of the most important business centres m the city. They have been complaining that on Saturdays they are not able to have their registered letters delivered to them before the banks close at the noon

Supply-Post Office
hour. If these letters were delivered earlier, business men could make their deposits before the banks close at noon. They also complain that these letters which they do not get on Saturday are not delivered until Monday afternoon. They ask for three mails a day instead of two, and a Saturday delivery before twelve o'clock. Has the matter been brought to the attention of the minister?
The matter is at present under investigation, and the representations of which the hon. member speaks will be considered before a decision is arrived at.

For a number of years Glace Bay has been looking for an extension of its town delivery. It is a large mining centre, with a population of about thirty to thirty-two thousand, and there is a partial system now installed which is working very well. Glace Bay is one of the best revenue producing cities which the department has. I understand the reason why the system has not been extended is that quite a number of the people have not fitted their doors with slots or receptacles in order to get the mail. I want to take this opportunity to point out to the departmental heads as well as to the minister that the people of Glace Bay have been promised this mail service for so many years that they have almost given up hope of getting it; and while quite a number have put in the slots or receptacles necessary for containing the mail, a great many others have not. I do not think it is fair to withhold the service from those who have equipped their doors, and I believe that if the department were to instal this service, say, any time to-morrow, those who have not equipped their doors to receive mail will do so within two or three days. They realize that the central portions of the town are efficiently served in this respect, but they say, " What is the use? We won't get it." I appeal to the minister to have the system installed, and I will guarantee that these people who only need to be convinced will certainly instal with alacrity their part of the equipment.
Mr. McLARTY; My understanding is that the only reason why the delivery system has not been installed was that it was required that fifty per cent of the residents along the route would instal slots in their doors. The purpose of the requirement is obvious. Without it, the mail carrier has to go round to the back-door; this results in inconvenience and delay in the mail, and it is unfair to those who do instal equipment. This is a matter in connection with which the department has
to observe some rules. We shall be glad to give consideration to the representations of the hon. member.

There is one other angle I should like the Postmaster General to bear in mind. As he must know, a great number of people in a large mining community are not so greatly interested in receiving their mail. It may be convenient for some of these people who receive only periodicals and an occasional letter to call at the main post office and get them: at the same time these people are depriving the vast majority of a daily delivery of mail. As I have said, if the department would instal the service and deliver the mail to those who have already equipped their doors with receptacles, the others would follow suit within a day or two.

There is a matter regarding superannuation which I should like to- bring to the minister's attention. Does he wish it brought up at this time, or would he .prefer that it be mentioned on another item?
Would it be peculiarly referable to the post office at all?

That was the point I wanted to bring up. It is in connection with the post office. I do not wish to refer to any particular case, just to the general question of the superannuation of post office employees.
I think the hon. member might as well do it now.

It is well known, I believe, that if any postal employee is for any reason dismissed for cause or dismissed as a result of some crime, and is imprisoned therefor, he loses his superannuation. I have in mind one or two particular cases, but I do not wish to refer to any name. This matter is, of course, statutory at the moment and the minister has no control; nevertheless it is worthwhile bringing it to his attention in view of the hardship caused dependents of an employee. After all, a misdemeanour on the part of an employee of the post office, punishable by a gaol sentence, is a serious matter. None of us will deny that. But when a man has served the Post Office Department for twenty or thirty years, and is within a few years of superannuation, and then for some reason or another he commits a crime and is incarcerated, his family are the ones who suffer and not himself. There have been such cases, as the minister knows. I do not wish to call attention to any one in particular, but I have drawn to the minister's attention certain cases and he has given them every
Supply-Post Office

possible consideration for which the families concerned are grateful, as I assure him I am.
At the time I discussed the matter with him this session he said he would take it into consideration with the thought perhaps of seeing what might be done to rectify a situation which would cause undue hardship to the family of a man who had been gaoled for a crime such as removing from the post office table an envelope containing money. A man may be with the post office as long as twenty-five years; he may have a wife and children; he is in mediocre circumstances, and as a result of some sudden temptation he removes an envelope and puts it in his pocket. He is sentenced to three years. He loses his superannuation-not only his superannuation, but all the money he has paid into the fund. It is lost to him for cause, it is true, but his family are the innocent victims. I have in mind one or two cases where there were several children. The father is removed from the family; there is no breadwinner; the mother may not be capable of working owing to some physical incapacity, and she finds herself destitute because her husband no longer earns any money and his superannuation is gone. All the money that he has paid into the fund over a period of years is lost not only to himself but to his wife as well. I was wondering whether the minister, after consideration of one or two particular cases, had any statement to make as to what progress he had made in this matter.

Offences of this sort do
not relate pecularily to the post office. They come under the Civil Service Superannuation Act, in connection with which there has been an investigation by a committee of this house for some time. The committee has since brought in its report. After all, it is not a matter that is referable to the post office as such. I greatly appreciate the hardship that reflects itself on the unfortunate family of the man who has been guilty of misconduct, but that is something which comes under the statute. In the administration of the Post Office Department my powers are strictly limited by acts of parliament I am here in an administrative capacity, and it is the duty of the house to make any amendment it deems desirable.

I am sure the minister
does not misunderstand the spirit in which I have brought up this matter-
Not at all.

-or the particular cases I had in mind. He went out of his way to

see what could be done, and those who were interested appreciated this as much as I did.

I regretted that I could
not do anything.

I understand that fully, but the minister will agree that a case of this sort might arise more readily in the Post Office Department than in any other. Here men are handling large sums of money daily, and the chances of such an occurrence are greater in the post office than in any other department. I wished to bring the matter to the attention of the committee and of the ministry as a whole because there does arise at times a situation which is grossly unfair to the unfortunate family concerned.

The same question arose in my own mind when I saw the larger figure paid to the Canadian Pacific. So far as the post office is concerned, in the carriage of mail

it must use that system which best serves the needs of the postal service. Seeing it is over ten years since the postal rates were established between the government and the railways, does the minister consider the time opportune to have a further reference to the transport board with a view to arranging new rates or another contract and saving money to the government?

And of course every hon. member who has any business with railways knows that express rates have been dropped materially because of bus and truck competition.
In regard to the other matter, I agree with my hon. friend that the only way for the post office to approach the problem of distribution of mail carriage between the two railways is to consider it from the point of view of the interests of the service. We cannot pick favourites, despite the fact that one happens to be a government owned railway. The primary object of the Post Office Department is to give the quickest and most efficient service possible, and let the railway which is able to provide that service secure the business, to which it is justly entitled under the circumstances.

For several years I have called the attention of the Postmaster General to what I consider a great hardship to the rural mail carriers in Canada. When a rural mail carrier is required, the position is advertised, tenders are asked for, and the position invariably goes to the lowest tenderer so long as he can procure two sureties satisfactory to the department. The contract is made for four years. At the end of that time the man who has the patronage of the riding, the member if his party is in office, or the defeated candidate if the party he supports is in office, is asked whether he will recommend renewal of this contract or whether it should be put up for tender. Here is a man who four years ago purchased a horse, cutter, buggy, harness and equipment. He now finds his contract is put up for tender; someone underbids him, and he is left with his horse and equipment, or car as the case may be, on his hands. No one objects to a government appointing its friends to positions. That is quite right. But when the man who takes that public position, ceases to be a partisan, and gives faithful and loyal service, I have always contended and contend to-day that he should not be removed except for cause. The man who has the patronage of the riding cannot say who is to get the mail contract, but he has the right to ask to have it put up for tender. And the carrier is underbid and ruthlessly thrown out of a position in which he has given faithful service.
Mail is delivered, in the cities also, but a different plan is followed there. When appli-
[M\ Green.]
cations for postmen in cities are invited, the salary is stated. The department select the man they consider most competent to discharge the duties of that position.
The commission selects him.

Yes, the commission. In the country, however, they are asked to compete against each other, and then they have no security in their position, for the contract expires at the end of four years. I would ask what I have asked on several previous occasions, that the rural mail carrier be placed in the same position as the city mail carrier. I do not think there should be any discrimination 'between them. These rural mail carriers are rendering a splendid service to the country, and there should be some stability about their positions.
I would suggest that a fair way to deal with the matter would be to place a value per mile on each route. Some routes can be run more economically than others. Some routes are along the highways, where the snow is kept ploughed in the winter and the road is kept in perfect shape. Generally these highways run through the more thickly settled parts of the country, and on those routes the mail can be delivered more cheaply than on country routes where the roads are not kept in the same condition. Put a value of $40, $45 or $50 a mile on these routes, according to their condition; invite applications for the position, stating what the salary will be, as is done in the cities. Then let the civil service commission select the man they consider most competent to discharge the duties of that office. I believe this change should be made.

The hon. member for
Lanark has covered the situation I tried to bring up under item 275, and I believe he has pretty well outlined what I wanted to say. I think a great injustice is being done some of our rural mail carriers, particularly in Saskatchewan where during the last two years many contracts have been thrown open at the end of the four year period. I know of men who have been carrying the mail for six or seven years, whose contracts were renewed four years ago. When those contracts expired this year, however, new tenders were called for and these men were thrown out. The hon. member for Lanark, however, has dealt with the matter so thoroughly that I need not say any more along that line.
I notice a considerable increase in this vote, and I wonder if the minister could break down that increase as between the air and

While I endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Lanark, there is one other aspect of this matter that I do not think has been touched. We now have the treasury department interfering in the prices paid on these rural routes. I had this situation drawn to my attention last fall. The treasury department raised objection to the continuation of one rural route, stating that since another route in the same constituency was being carried on for something like $35 a mile, they would refuse to allow a further contract for the other rural route because it was costing $41 a mile. There is something seriously wrong in that situation. We have a new minister in the department, and I would suggest to him that now is the time to take a club to the treasury department, before he gets too seasoned in office. If he does not deal with them the situation never will be altered. In good faith the Post Office Department calls for tenders and, as the hon. member for Lanark pointed out, the tender goes to the lowest bidder, very often at a price far below cost. That policy having been adopted, however, why should the treasury department step in and say that because one man has taken a route at $35 a mile, another man fifteen miles away will have to take his route for $35 also? I do not know how many hon. members have had this situation drawn to their attention, but I know it was .brought to mine and I made up my mind that I would air this grievance on the floor of the house. It is the treasury department that is doing this, not the Post Office Department. We have
growing up in this country a higher officialdom which, if it is not controlled to some extent, will become our very masters. I warn hon. members to protest on every occasion against interference by the treasury department. In 1933 we had this department interfering with the pensions of the returned men, when they did not know the first thing about the individual pensioners. We now have them interfering in rural mail contracts. I urge upon the minister that now is the time to assert his authority, and that once a contract has been let, that price should be maintained.

During the last three years I have listened to certain remarks by my hon. friends to the left concerning the opening of certain contracts by members supporting the government, suggesting that this was rather a drastic step to take and that probably politics were mixed up in it in some way. The insinuation has been there.
It is quite true, too.

I said last year, and I repeat, that so far as I am concerned in my own riding I have never carried on any such tactics, in connection with rural mail routes, as were carried on between 1930 and 1935. I know of one contract that was let, the amount of which was increased each year without new tenders being called. That is in the records of the department, and that took place under the Conservative government.
That was generous treatment.

Yes, it was generous treatment on the part of the former Postmaster General.
Passing from that, however, and without any desire to play politics in connection with this matter of mail contracts-keeping away from politics altogether-I should like to say a -word on behalf of the rural mail carriers of Canada. We hear very little about these people, yet I believe they are closer to the rural home life of our country than perhaps any other employees of the dominion government. We have approximately 4,500 employees operating these routes at a total cost, in round figures, of $2,700,000. I have obtained figures showing the cost per mile from December, 1922, to December, 1937. I shall not place all the figures on record, but I believe it would be sufficient to say that on December 31, 1922, the average cost per mile on mail routes was $41.37, and that this amount gradually decreased until on December 31, 1937, the average price was only $32.47, or a drastic reduction of about $9 on what might be described as very small contracts yielding small remuneration.
